Yes, `std::string myString;` **does call the default constructor** in C++11 (and all versions of C++).

This declaration creates a `std::string` object named `myString` and initializes it by calling the default constructor `std::string()`, which creates an empty string (with length 0).

This is equivalent to:
```cpp
std::string myString{};  // C++11 uniform initialization
std::string myString(""); // Explicit empty string
std::string myString = std::string(); // Explicit default construction
```

All of these create an empty string object. The default constructor is always called for class types when you declare a variable without an initializer - this is different from built-in types like `int`, which would be left uninitialized in some contexts.

So after `std::string myString;`, you have a valid, empty string object that you can safely use:
```cpp
std::string myString;
std::cout << myString.length();  // Prints: 0
std::cout << myString.empty();   // Prints: 1 (true)
```
